f_fundamental_hz.conditions: Internal auto-calibration (chopper) rate. The datasheet states the time-continuous 350-kHz signal-path amplifier is 'zero-corrected every 8 us'; 125 kHz is that 8 us period expressed as a frequency. TI publishes no amplitude for the resulting switching artifact and states the architecture has no aliasing or flicker noise.

thermal.accuracy_note: Not a temperature sensor, but its accuracy is temperature-gradient sensitive in a way that matters for placement: the datasheet warns that thermoelectric (Seebeck) junctions formed by dissimilar conductors generate 0.1 uV/C or more, against a 10 uV maximum input offset voltage. A gradient of only a few degrees across the two input terminals is therefore comparable to the part's entire offset budget.

conducted.reason: ECG signal band. TI's own single-supply, very-low-power ECG circuit built around this device (Figure 33) sets fHPF = 0.5 Hz and fLPF = 150 Hz, so this is the vendor's stated passband for this part in this application.

noise_floor.conditions: Input voltage noise, f = 0.1 Hz to 10 Hz, TA = 25 C (0.3 uVpp over 0.01 Hz to 1 Hz)

cmrr_db.conditions: (V-) - 0.1 V < VCM < (V+) + 0.1 V, TA = -40 C to 125 C; 106 dB minimum

design_notes.note: Thermal gradients across the two input terminals are a first-order error source. Dissimilar-metal junctions produce thermoelectric potentials of 0.1 uV/C or more against a 10 uV max offset spec, so the amplifier and its input network must be thermally isolated from power supplies and other heat sources, shielded from air currents, and laid out so both inputs sit at the same temperature.

Run the input traces as far away from the supply lines as possible, and place the gain-setting components close to the device and to each other to reduce parasitic errors. Use a low-ESR ceramic bypass capacitor (0.1 uF) directly across the supply pins.

RFI susceptibility shows up as a shift in offset voltage or DC level with the interfering RF signal. The OPA333 is specifically designed to minimise RFI susceptibility, but TI still warns that strong RF fields can cause varying offset levels -- relevant on a board that also carries a 2.4 GHz transmitter.

Power-supply rejection is specified as 1 uV/V typ, 5 uV/V max over VS = 1.8 V to 5.5 V and -40 C to 125 C -- i.e. referred to the input, not in dB. A 100 mV rail excursion becomes at most 0.5 uV of input-referred error, which is small against the 1.1 uVpp 0.1-10 Hz noise floor.

Input terminals are diode-clamped to the rails. Input signals that can swing more than 0.3 V beyond the supply rails must be current limited to 10 mA or less (a series resistor), which matters for electrode nets exposed to defibrillation or ESD.

provenance.notes: Datasheet covers OPA333 (single) and OPA2333 (dual). Only the three OPA333 packages (D SOIC, DBV SOT-23, DCK SC70) are recorded in theta_ja; the OPA2333 table on the same page adds DGK VSSOP (180.3 C/W) and DRB VSON (46.7 C/W) if the dual is used instead. Mechanical records the DBV SOT-23-5. psrr_db is deliberately absent: TI specifies PSRR for this part in uV/V (1 typ, 5 max), not in dB, and converting it would manufacture a number -- the raw figure is kept verbatim in design_notes. The 125 kHz conducted-emission entry is the reciprocal of the datasheet's stated 8 us auto-zero interval; the datasheet never prints a chopping frequency or an artifact amplitude, so ripple is absent. The susceptibility band 0.5-150 Hz comes from TI's own ECG application circuit on page 22, not from a generic assumption. No radiated emissions: passive analog part, no transmitter.
